name: Work instructions and manufacturing SOPs
one_line: Controlled type-level instructions that tell an operator how to perform one manufacturing operation: ordered steps, setup and tooling, parameter limits, in-process checks, safety controls, revision/effective-date control and approval. It is not the executed batch record, engineering specification, warehouse procedure or generic corporate policy merely because those files also contain numbered steps.

node_test.why: The manufacturing schema default recognizes recurring transformation or control cycles: executed production, inspection, nonconformance, calibration, maintenance and HSE records. This template is type-level and prospective: a controlled instruction has an operation or station scope, ordered steps, setup/tooling, specified parameter ranges, checkpoints, safety controls, document revision, effective date and approval, but no instance-specific actuals, lot genealogy or returned-to-service result. Its recommended organization is product/process or site/station → record type, with document revision retained as version-family evidence rather than a folder level; this differs from the default's product → batch/lot, site → asset and quality-event branches. Privacy is also distinct in concentration: the instruction can disclose the repeatable process recipe, machine settings, access restrictions and worker-safety controls even when no particular lot has been made. The row remains fieldless because PR-6 defers manufacturing fields. If R1c decides work instructions are only the `work instruction` value already named in the manufacturing schema and cannot preserve this type-versus-instance distinction, refusal is required.

deterministic: a controlled instruction with a labelled document or procedure number, revision, effective date, owner/approver and scope identifying one product, process, operation, station or machine

an ordered step table or flowchart whose rows tell an operator what to do, what tool or material to use, what parameter or range to set, and what check or decision follows; the sequence and imperative operation relation are the signal
a setup sheet that joins a station or machine, tooling/fixture identity, setup sequence, specified parameter ranges, first-piece or in-process check and signoff/approval, with no actual lot values

a standard operating procedure whose manufacturing scope, line or equipment anchor and controlled revision block are explicit, and whose body describes repeatable execution rather than a one-time result
a cleaning, sanitation, line-clearance, changeover or lockout procedure tied to a product/process or production asset, with preconditions, ordered actions, verification and release steps

an embedded operator instruction inside a controlled production document or manufacturing-system export, where the instruction's own revision/effective control and type-level steps are distinguishable from the order's actual execution data

a controlled visual work aid with annotated operation photographs or diagrams, station/tool labels, numbered actions, parameter limits and approval/effective metadata; a photograph or diagram alone is not enough

a training or competence package only when its content reproduces a controlled manufacturing instruction for one operation and carries the instruction's revision/effective reference; a general training deck is not this row

an email or calendar item whose native fields and attachment manifest announce release, withdrawal, review or training of a named manufacturing instruction, while the message alone remains a group member rather than proof of the instruction's body

an archive manifest linking one controlled instruction revision to setup sheets, visual aids, checklists, change notices and withdrawn copies; the archive is inspected through its manifest without unpacking

whether a document is type-level and reusable or an instance-level traveller whose blank-looking cells are actually missing execution evidence
whether a procedure is controlled by the manufacturing organization or is a supplier manual, customer specification, regulator document or public safety guidance
whether an instruction's product, process, station or machine anchor is sufficiently explicit when the title only says SOP, standard work or operation
whether a setup table containing ranges and measured first-piece values is an instruction plus a production/inspection record, or only a completed batch record with copied procedure text
whether an OCR-poor scan preserves numbered steps, parameter labels, checkboxes, revision control and station scope well enough to activate
whether a screenshot of a MES or quality portal shows the controlled instruction itself, a release workflow, or merely a search result and should be grouped without copying facts
whether a work instruction is also a corporate policy or compliance procedure when the same bytes carry both a shop-floor operation and an organization-wide obligation
whether a maintenance or calibration method is an instruction for operators or an asset-specific work order/certificate whose evidence is the performed service
whether a multilingual or highly abbreviated shop-floor document can be interpreted without turning a guessed operation, parameter or approval state into a fact
never_alone: the words work instruction, WI, SOP, standard work, procedure, method, router, traveller, setup, operation, process, manufacturing, production, quality or shop floor alone
a product, part, machine, line, station, plant, operator, supplier or organization name alone
a document number, revision, effective date, work-order number, operation code or serial-like token outside a labelled controlled-document and scope structure
numbered steps, imperative verbs, a flowchart, a parameter table, a checklist, a signature, an approval stamp or a safety warning alone
a specified temperature, pressure, torque, speed, tolerance, quantity, time or pass/fail value alone; these occur in specifications, records, manuals and test reports
a source_type or extension alone, including PDF, DOCX, spreadsheet, image, OCR, presentation, email, calendar, archive, JSON or design file
a parent folder called SOPs, Work Instructions, Procedures, Manufacturing, Quality, Operations, Plant or Training alone

a download, release, review or training session alone; 00 says: "A session should never be treated as proof of topic, and it should not carry the same confidence as a hash match or a directly extracted document fact."
a product or machine photograph, screenshot, diagram, QR code or barcode without a controlled instruction structure

a blank form or blank traveller with the same step grid and parameter table but no instance identifier, actual values, effective control or approved scope; it may be a template, not an active instruction

lockout, safety and emergency operating instruction

grouping_reasons: one controlled operation across its current and superseded instruction revisions, setup sheets, visual aids and release/withdrawal records; version_family remains the universal relation

one product, process, station or machine across reusable instructions and the executed production, inspection or maintenance groups that reference them, without copying the instruction's product or station facts onto those members
one changeover or line-clearance procedure across its checklist, release evidence, training reference and related controlled change
one special process across its normative specification, operator instruction, qualification evidence and completed batch records; the same bytes may support separate templates on disjoint evidence
one instruction release cycle across approval, effective-date notice, controlled-copy distribution, training acknowledgement and withdrawal evidence
a sparse screenshot, email, calendar event or photograph may join an accepted instruction group without receiving product, operation, revision or station facts from neighbours
a document that is both a corporate policy and a shop-floor instruction can retain both evidence relations; placement is decided later and neither group may propagate labels

template.why: Empty because manufacturing is a PR-6 placeholder and declares no legal destination fields. Subject to R1c, this situation recommends product or process → site/station or machine → record type, with site optional for a single-plant corpus and revision handled by universal version_family rather than a branch. A procedure is reusable across many batches, so batch_lot is deliberately omitted; a production traveller owns the executed order/lot, and a specification owns normative requirements. Time is not first: 00 states, "For document and record domains, project, function, or subject usually comes before time because putting year first scatters related work across calendar folders." The user may reverse, remove, add or flatten any eventual order. No operation, parameter, tool, worker, customer or document number is proposed as a destination dimension until R1c resolves the canonical vocabulary and privacy consequences.

collides_with.signal: SAME FIXTURE BYTES: `Setup sheet OP30 AX-410 rev C.pdf` and the same parameter table embedded in `BPR_AX410_L240817-03.pdf`. Direction one — manufacturing.work-instruction owns the TYPE-level controlled instruction: document number, revision, effective date, approver, operation/station scope, ordered steps, tooling and specified parameter ranges with no one-lot actuals. Direction two — manufacturing.production-record owns the INSTANCE-level execution: one order or batch/lot identifier, actual values and timestamps per operation, operator signoffs, issued/good/scrap or rework reconciliation and release disposition. The procedure text can appear in both bytes; a parameter range, product name, lot-shaped token or signoff alone discriminates neither. This row must not take the traveller's actuals merely because it embeds the procedure, and production-record must not take a reusable setup sheet merely because it names a product and operation.

SAME FIXTURE BYTES: `PS-217 Rev 3 - Solution Heat Treat and Age.docx`. Direction one — manufacturing.work-instruction owns an operator-facing, ordered execution instruction for one station or operation, with setup/tooling, specified ranges, checks and controlled release. Direction two — engineering.material-specification owns the normative process definition: requirements, allowable ranges, qualification method, referenced standards, sampling and what the process must achieve across many jobs. A temperature, time, process name, revision or approval block alone allocates neither; this row must not take the specification simply because it includes steps, and material-specification must not take a shop instruction merely because it repeats a requirement. The separate fixture `Furnace 2 - Load and Unload Steps Rev B.docx` is the instruction-side negative where station and per-load sequence are explicit.

SAME FIXTURE BYTES: `Pick-Pack Standard Work - Bay 3.pdf`. Direction one — manufacturing.work-instruction owns a controlled instruction whose operation transforms, assembles, tests or controls a product at a manufacturing station, with process parameters, tooling/material inputs and in-process checks. Direction two — logistics.warehouse-ops owns the facility's internal custody work: pick, pack, scan, bin, handling-unit and outbound-wave steps, with no product transformation or manufacturing release. A numbered sequence, item code, bay, revision or operator audience alone allocates neither; this row must not claim warehouse standard work from the phrase SOP, and warehouse-ops must not claim a manufacturing setup or assembly instruction merely because goods are handled at a station.

SAME FIXTURE BYTES: `SOP-014 Goods receipt.docx`. Direction one — manufacturing.work-instruction owns a shop-floor instruction tied to a product/process, machine/station and in-process control, telling an operator the ordered execution steps. Direction two — business_operations.policy-handbook owns an organization-wide governing procedure whose scope, responsibilities, obligations, document control and review cycle bind a population or administrative process. Numbered steps, responsibility columns, revision history and the word SOP alone allocate neither; this row must not take an administrative procedure merely because it is called standard work, and policy-handbook must not take a manufacturing execution instruction merely because it is controlled and procedural.

SAME FIXTURE BYTES: `Irrigation-Pump-Commissioning-Pack_Field-12.zip` is the analogous controlled-package fixture, and `Process map - Operator Steps.svg` is the shared visual-aid form. Direction one — manufacturing.work-instruction owns a reusable operator procedure for a manufacturing station or process, with steps, ranges, tooling and in-process checks. Direction two — engineering.commissioning-handover owns installed-instance acceptance: as-built identity, test results, settings, punch-list closure, witnessed acceptance and transfer to an operator. A step diagram, machine tag, parameter, handover word or approval alone allocates neither; this row must not take an acceptance pack merely because operators receive it, and commissioning-handover must not take a type-level procedure merely because it is used during startup.

falls_through_to.why: A standalone controlled instruction, setup sheet or durable SOP with no accepted product/process group can remain a meaningful record without forcing an unlicensed manufacturing hierarchy.

A readable sequence, parameter workbook, visual aid or mixed procedure packet whose manufacturing, engineering, logistics or business role cannot be established from its own evidence is partly understood and should remain unresolved.
An isolated release email, review calendar item, controlled-copy notice or training confirmation without the instruction body is a transaction or confirmation, not proof of this template.

A supplier manual, safety data sheet, public standard, consumer assembly booklet or general operating guide with no local controlled-process relation is reference material rather than a manufacturing instruction.
A photograph of a machine, tool, operator or annotated page with no legible controlled-document relation and no accepted instruction group remains an unassociated image.

Instructions and release packets may disclose proprietary process recipes, machine settings, access controls, worker names, safety controls and customer-specific production methods. When no deeper group is accepted, protected review avoids creating a revealing branch.
An encrypted MES export, proprietary document container or unreadable scan is represented safely from metadata and cannot activate from a work-instruction-shaped filename.

sensitivity_why: A work instruction concentrates the repeatable process recipe: machine settings, ranges, tooling, fixtures, material sequence, quality checkpoints, safety interlocks and sometimes customer-specific methods or named operators. That exposure differs from a generic manufacturing pile because the instruction can teach the process independently of any one lot, while a release/training packet can also contain worker identities and access restrictions. The row therefore remains potentially_sensitive, keeps raw parameters and worker names out of destination dimensions, and prefers bounded local evidence. It assigns no handling class; P7 owns that vocabulary.
open_question: NEEDS-JOSEPH NJ-WI-1: is the type-versus-instance boundary sufficient to keep this row distinct from manufacturing.production-record, or should both be one work_type family under the manufacturing default? Keep this row only if reusable controlled instructions can be detected without claiming executed actuals. NJ-WI-2: should the canonical manufacturing vocabulary reuse the anchor's proposed `product`, `site`, `asset` and global `record_type`, with operation/station remaining a value or search facet, or is a neutral process/operation key needed globally? This row proposes no key. NJ-WI-3: where one file is both a shop-floor instruction and a business-wide SOP, should R1c lift resource/schema coactivation between manufacturing and business_operations or let template-level evidence remain independently scoped? Templates cannot author `also_holds_with`. NJ-WI-4: where a special-process specification and an operator instruction repeat the same ranges, should both schemas/templates coactivate on disjoint normative versus executional evidence, or should one side own the shared document and the other only the group? NJ-WI-5: should instruction revisions remain only in universal `version_family`, or may a future user-confirmed private tree expose controlled revision/effective state? NJ-WI-6: when a training deck, email or screenshot names an instruction but lacks the body, should accepted-group context be enough for membership while all instruction facts remain unknown?
